at undskylde.explanation: "At undskylde" means to apologize, and also to excuse. The short phrase "Undskyld" means both "Sorry" and "Excuse me", which is handy when you want to get past someone or get a waiter's attention. To say you are sorry for something, use "Jeg undskylder for ...".

sentence.da: Jeg **undskylder** for at komme for sent.

en uge.explanation: En uge is a week. In Danish, "the week" is "ugen", and more than one is "uger". Danes often use week numbers in daily life, for example "uge 42", especially at work and in school. Useful phrases are "i næste uge" (next week) and "i denne uge" (this week).

en ugedag.explanation: "En ugedag" is a day of the week, such as Monday or Friday. It is built from "uge" (week) and "dag" (day). It can also mean a working day, as opposed to the weekend. All days of the week are written with a small letter in Danish.

sentence.en: Which day of the week is it today?

et udsalg.explanation: "Et udsalg" is a sale, a period when a shop sells things at lower prices, for example after Christmas or in the summer. You can say "Der er udsalg" (There is a sale). It is not the same as "et tilbud", which is a single deal on one thing. The plural is the same as the single word.

sentence.en: I bought the jacket at the sale.

et ur.explanation: "Et ur" means both a clock and a watch. Context shows which you mean. A watch on the wrist can be said "et armbåndsur" (wrist watch), and a wall one "et vægur". Do not mix it up with "klokken", which is used for telling the time: "Hvad er klokken?".

forms.en: He goes out of the house.
I go out into the garden.

ud.explanation: "Ud" means "out" and is used when something moves from inside to outside, as in "Kom ud!" (Come out!). For being outside, Danes say "ude". "Ud" is also in everyday phrases, like "at gå ud" (to go out, for example in the evening) and "Hvordan ser det ud?" (What does it look like?). Its opposite is "ind" (in).

sentence.en: We go out into the garden.

uden.explanation: "Uden" means without. Before an action you say "uden at": "uden at spise" (without eating). It is the opposite of "med" (with). Do not mix it up with "udenfor", which means outside. It is a short, very common word that you will use daily when ordering food and drink.

udenfor.explanation: "Udenfor" means outside, and it works both for where something is and for going out: "Vi er udenfor" and "Vi går udenfor". The opposite is "indenfor" (inside). It is sometimes written as two words, "uden for".

udsolgt.explanation: "Udsolgt" means sold out, with none left to buy. You see it on a shelf, on a website or at a concert. It is made of "ud" (out) and "solgt" (sold). Add an "e" when it describes more than one thing, as in "udsolgte billetter".

ugift.explanation: "Ugift" means unmarried or single in the legal sense, the opposite of "gift". The little word "u-" in front turns a word into its opposite, as in "uvenlig" (unfriendly). On forms you may see "gift / ugift" as the choice for your status.

ukraine.explanation: "Ukraine" is Ukraine. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i Ukraine" means "in Ukraine" and "til Ukraine" means "to Ukraine". A person is "en ukrainer" and the language is "ukrainsk". The word is spelled the same as in English.

ukrainsk.explanation: "Ukrainsk" means Ukrainian, for people, things and the language. It is written with a small letter and does not change before an et-word. The country is "Ukraine" and a person from there is "en ukrainer".

sentence.en: My colleague speaks Ukrainian and Danish.

under.explanation: "Under" means under or below, and it also means during: "under krigen" (during the war). It is also used for amounts smaller than something. The opposite is "over". Learn it together with its opposite so you remember both directions.

sentence.en: The cat sleeps under the bed.

underbukser.explanation: "Underbukser" means underpants. It is always used in this form, with more than one, just like "bukser". It is built from "under" (under) and "bukser" (pants). For one pair, say "et par underbukser". Danes also say "trusser" for women's underwear.

undertøj.explanation: "Undertøj" means underwear. It is an et-word and, like "tøj" (clothes), it is a collective word that is not used in the plural. You say "undertøjet" for the underwear. It is made of "under" (under) and "tøj" (clothes), so it is easy to remember.

sentence.en: I need to buy new underwear.

forms.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

undskyld.explanation: "Undskyld" means both "sorry" and "excuse me". You use it to apologise, as in "Undskyld, jeg kom for sent" (Sorry, I came too late), and to get someone's attention politely, as in "Undskyld, må jeg komme forbi?" (Excuse me, may I get past?). As a question, "Undskyld?" means "Pardon?" when you didn't hear. It is one word, with sk in the middle.

sentence.en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

forms.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

undskyld mig.explanation: "Undskyld mig" means "excuse me" and gets someone's attention or lets you pass. It can also be shortened to "undskyld", which means both "excuse me" and "sorry". Use it to ask a stranger for help or to say sorry for a small mistake.

sentence.en: Excuse me, may I get past?

ung.explanation: "Ung" means young. It is the opposite of "gammel" (old). The word "unge" is also used on its own to mean young people, as in "de unge" (the young ones). Add "t" for et-words ("et ungt par") and "-e" for more than one. For a very small child Danes say "lille" or "et barn" instead.

usa.explanation: "USA" is the USA. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i USA" means "in the USA" and "til USA" means "to the USA". It is said as three letters, "u-es-a". Danes write it in capitals and use it without "the": "i USA" means "in the USA". A person is "en amerikaner", and "amerikansk" describes things from there.

sentence.en: My sister lives in the USA.

usund.explanation: "Usund" means unhealthy and is the opposite of "sund". The "u" at the front gives the opposite meaning, as in many Danish words. It adds a "t" with et-words ("usundt") and an "e" for more than one ("usunde"). It describes food, habits or lifestyles.
